title: Neighbor-Joining, by hand
summary: Work a small distance matrix like a paper exercise: predict the join, then watch NJ make it.

objectives: Predict which pair Neighbor-Joining joins from a small distance matrix
Explain why the closest pair is not always the pair NJ joins first
Recognize a tied join that leaves the tree unchanged

source.citation: Constructed for NeoPhylo: the textbook five-taxon Neighbor-Joining example matrix (the one in the Wikipedia article 'Neighbor joining') with one cell changed so the closest pair is not joined first

prompts.concept: A distance matrix alone is enough to build a tree — no sequences needed. This one is small enough to work by hand, like a paper exercise: predict the first join, then step through — the later joins are explained as they happen.
prompts.math: With a supplied matrix there is no correction step — the numbers in the cells are the distances the methods work on directly.

prompts.concept: Neighbor-Joining starts from the distance matrix. Which two taxa join first? Work out Q for the pairs before you pick.
prompts.math: NJ joins the pair minimizing Q(i,j) = (n−2)·d(i,j) − R_i − R_j. Work the Q scores out by hand — the smallest one wins.
prompts.reveal: a and b join first even though d and e sit closest in the matrix: a and b are each farther from everything else, and the Q score subtracts exactly that. Now switch the matrix to Q to check your working.

prompts.concept: The join you just passed had a hidden tie: joining c to the cluster made in the first join scored exactly the same on Q as joining d and e. When two tied pairs are complements — together they cover every active cluster — either choice builds the same split, so the tie changes nothing. NeoPhylo picks the first tied pair in scan order.
prompts.math: At four active clusters, a pair and its complement that share the minimum Q always resolve to the same unrooted split — an ambiguous tie, by contrast, would change the tree.

prompts.concept: The tree is complete — and the first join was not the closest pair. NJ's Q score subtracts each taxon's total divergence from the rest, so a pair that looks close can still lose to a pair whose members sit far from everything else. That is the point of the method: it joins on relative closeness, not raw distance.
prompts.math: Q(i,j) = (n−2)·d(i,j) − R_i − R_j: the row sums R_i and R_j are each cluster's total divergence, and subtracting them is what let the winner beat the smallest cell.
